art.alt: An engraved neural network cutaway reveals sparse activation paths under scientific probes.
art.prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept
Asset type: wide 16:9 editorial series plate for a serious long-form knowledge garden
Primary request: a cutaway view through a deep neural network as an interpretability instrument: layered computational planes recede across the page while only a few sparse activation paths illuminate in oxide red; delicate probe needles, feature lenses, attribution traces, and small circuit motifs reveal different scales from individual units to distributed features to connected circuits. It should feel like opening a precision scientific instrument whose internal causal pathways remain only partly visible.
Scene/backdrop: warm cream rag paper with faint laboratory-grid and translucent vellum overlays
Subject: abstract neural network cutaway, sparse activation paths, probes and circuit motifs; no brain silhouette and no anthropomorphic machine
Style/medium: original tactile printmaking, copperplate engraving, technical cutaway drawing and translucent scientific drafting layers, serious literary-scientific editorial illustration
Composition/framing: cinematic wide 16:9; left-to-right depth through network layers with a clear sparse path weaving across them; dense center, quieter margins; coherent single plate
Lighting/mood: forensic, patient, exacting, intellectually luminous without spectacle
Color palette: cream paper, charcoal black, oxide red, with one restrained teal-blue accent
Materials/textures: paper grain, etched hatching, dry ink, translucent tracing paper, fine instrument metal and glass
Constraints: textless; no letters, numbers, captions, logos, interface UI, or watermark; visual hierarchy must distinguish neuron/feature/circuit scales without labels
Avoid: generic sci-fi, neon, glowing holograms, humanoid robots, brain icons, stock circuit-board imagery, glossy 3D rendering, named-artist imitation

visuals.title: Why one neuron is usually the wrong grain
visuals.caption: Mechanistic interpretability moves from often-polysemantic neurons to distributed features and then to circuits whose causal role can be tested.

items.label: Neuron
items.detail: One activation value often responds to several unrelated concepts at once.

items.label: Feature
items.detail: A direction across many activations can track one concept hidden by superposition.

items.label: Circuit
items.detail: Connected features form an algorithm whose causal role can be tested by intervention.

visuals.title: The hidden intermediate in Dallas → Austin
visuals.caption: An attribution graph earns mechanistic status by exposing Texas as an intermediate feature and changing the answer when that feature is replaced.

items.label: Prompt feature
items.detail: “Dallas” activates an internal representation tied to the city named in the question.

items.label: Latent bridge
items.detail: The graph reveals “Texas,” a concept absent from the prompt but causally active inside the model.

items.label: Capital relation
items.detail: Texas combines with the capital relation to promote “Austin” at the output.

items.label: Counterfactual patch
items.detail: Replacing Texas with California changes the answer to Sacramento.

items.label: Second patch
items.detail: Replacing it with Byzantium changes the answer to Constantinople.

visuals.title: Sparse autoencoders survived by shrinking their claim
visuals.caption: In two years, the field moved from a hoped-for true dictionary of model concepts to a bounded discovery instrument with seed dependence and downstream limits attached.

items.label: Untangle superposition
items.detail: An SAE rewrites dense activity as a sparse combination of many learned directions.

items.label: Scale the dictionary
items.detail: Gemma Scope and frontier-model work learn millions of features across layers, some of them human-recognizable.

items.label: Test downstream use
items.detail: On DeepMind's harmful-intent task, a simple dense probe beats SAE-based probes, including out of distribution.

items.label: Repeat the lens
items.detail: Changing random seeds yields materially different decompositions; one studied setting shares only about 30% of features.

items.label: Separate discovery from control
items.detail: If you know the concept, start with a probe; if you do not, use the SAE to surface candidates you might not have named.

items.label: Keep the uncertainty
items.detail: Interpretable, steerable features are real, while their status as the model's native units remains unsettled.

visuals.title: The interpretability instrument moved from vision units to measured self-report
visuals.caption: The twenty-paper arc widens its object of study while every new instrument also reveals a new limitation.

items.label: Learning to see
items.detail: Curve detectors, logit lenses, and transformer components establish that internal structure can be read.

items.label: Behavior to mechanism
items.detail: Induction heads, fact editing, superposition, and task circuits make intervention central.

items.label: Worlds and algorithms
items.detail: Othello state, grokking, automated discovery, and function vectors expose richer computations.

items.label: Dictionary wave
items.detail: Sparse methods learn millions of features in frontier systems; only a subset are recognizably conceptual.

items.label: Biology and self-report
items.detail: Attribution graphs trace planning and unfaithful reasoning; concept injection probes introspection.

visuals.title: How the repeated-token probe locates an induction head
visuals.caption: A synthetic repeated sequence creates a precise attention signature you can score and then test by ablation.

items.label: Build the repeat
items.detail: Sample 25 random tokens and concatenate the same 25-token sequence a second time.

items.label: Read attention
items.detail: For every GPT-2 small layer and head, inspect the cached attention pattern.

items.label: Score the stripe
items.detail: Measure attention from each second-pass position back by an offset of 24.

items.label: Name candidates
items.detail: Heads with a mean score above 0.4 become candidates; published demos often flag layers 5–7.

items.label: Test causality
items.detail: Zero-ablate the high-scoring heads and check whether the repeated-sequence loss advantage shrinks.

visuals.title: The 2024 wave scaled sparse features—and exposed what one-dimensional entries miss
visuals.caption: The year's papers move from feature-level causal graphs to frontier-scale dictionaries, then force the unit of interpretation open again with dark matter, proxy metrics, and circular representations.

items.label: Trace with features
items.detail: Sparse Feature Circuits replaces opaque heads with SAE features and lets a human remove a gender shortcut from a classifier.

items.label: Scale to a frontier model
items.detail: Millions of Claude 3 Sonnet features include a multilingual, multimodal Golden Gate Bridge direction that causally steers behavior.

items.label: Industrialize the dictionary
items.detail: TopK methods support a 16-million-latent SAE trained on GPT-4 activations over 40 billion tokens.

items.label: Carry the missing mass
items.detail: Reconstruction and explainability scores are proxies, and large portions of the representation remain dark matter.

items.label: Break the straight line
items.detail: Days and months occupy irreducibly two-dimensional circles that the model uses for modular date arithmetic.

items.label: Reopen the object
items.detail: A useful dictionary decomposes activity, but decomposition alone does not prove that its entries are the model's true computational atoms.
